lines.text:
Thread, Needle, and Precision — The Art of the Tailor

A tailor shop is a quiet, focused place. A sewing machine hums in the background. Fabric rolls line the shelves. A dress form — a body-shaped stand — wears a half-finished jacket. A tape measure hangs from the tailor's neck. The work is slow, precise, and personal — every garment is made to fit one body.

The tailor's tools are simple but essential. A needle and thread do the hand-stitching. A bobbin holds thread inside the sewing machine. A thimble protects the finger when pushing a needle through thick fabric. A pin cushion holds straight pins that keep fabric in place before sewing. A seam ripper removes mistakes — unpicking stitches one by one. Sewing scissors cut fabric cleanly. A rotary cutter — a round blade on a handle — cuts straight lines on a cutting mat. A ruler and a tape measure ensure accuracy. A T-square draws right angles. A French curve — a curved ruler — helps draw armholes and necklines.

Before cutting, the tailor works with a pattern — a paper template of each piece. A fabric marker or chalk draws the cutting lines on the fabric. The pattern includes markings for darts — small folds that shape fabric to follow the curves of the body — and for the seam, the line where two pieces of fabric are stitched together.

Fabrics vary in weight, texture, and purpose. Cotton is breathable and easy to sew — ideal for shirts and summer clothes. Silk is smooth and luxurious — used for formal wear. Wool is warm and durable — common in suits and winter coats. Linen is light and cool — popular in hot climates. Denim is tough — the fabric of jeans. Leather is used for jackets and bags. Chiffon is sheer and delicate — used in evening dresses. Polyester is cheap and wrinkle-resistant. Velvet is soft and rich. Corduroy has a ribbed texture.

Fastenings hold a garment together. A button passes through a buttonhole. A zipper opens and closes with a slider. A hook and eye is a small metal fastener used where buttons would be too bulky. A snap clicks together with pressure. A buckle adjusts a belt or strap. Ribbon decorates. Lace adds elegance. An elastic band provides stretch. Velcro sticks to itself. Bias tape finishes raw edges.

Every garment has named parts. A collar frames the neck. A sleeve covers the arm. A cuff finishes the end of the sleeve. A hem is the finished bottom edge. A pocket holds small items. A lapel folds back on a jacket front. A waistband sits at the waist of trousers or a skirt. A seam joins two pieces of fabric. A dart shapes the fabric to fit the body.

A mannequin in the shop window displays the finished product. The tailor checks the fit — adjusting a hem here, taking in a seam there. The garment is pressed with a steam iron.

In a world of fast fashion, a tailor offers something rare: clothing made for you, by someone who understands how fabric, body, and design come together.

lines.text: Welcome. What can I make for you today?
lines.name: Welcome. What can I make for you today?

lines.text: I need a suit for a formal event. Something classic — maybe wool or linen?
lines.name: I need a suit for a formal event. Something classic — maybe wool or linen?

lines.text: Wool is excellent for structure. Linen is lighter but creases more easily. Let me take your measurements first. Stand on the platform near the dress form.
lines.name: Wool is excellent for structure. Linen is lighter but creases more easily. Let me take your measurements first. Stand on the platform near the dress form.

lines.text: Yes, please. I'll use the tape measure for your chest, shoulders, waist, and sleeve length. I'll mark everything with chalk on the pattern.
lines.name: Yes, please. I'll use the tape measure for your chest, shoulders, waist, and sleeve length. I'll mark everything with chalk on the pattern.

lines.text: What's that curved ruler on the table?
lines.name: What's that curved ruler on the table?

lines.text: A French curve — I use it for drawing smooth necklines and armholes on the pattern. The T-square is for straight lines.

lines.text: Can you show me the fabric options?

lines.text: Of course. We have cotton, silk, wool, linen, denim for casual wear, and polyester blends. For a formal suit, I'd recommend this wool. Feel the weight.

lines.text: That's perfect. How long will it take?

lines.text: 'Break – broke – broken.' 'Broke' = past simple: 'The zip broke yesterday.' 'Broken' = past participle (used with 'is/has'): 'The zip is broken.' 'I have broken a button.' Never use the past simple form after 'is/has/have.'

lines.text: ❌ "She sewed the button in my shirt yesterday."
lines.name: ❌ "She sewed the button in my shirt yesterday."

lines.text: ✅ "She sewed the button on my shirt yesterday." / "She sewed the button onto my shirt."
lines.name: ✅ "She sewed the button on my shirt yesterday." / "She sewed the button onto my shirt."

lines.text: Buttons go 'on' or 'onto' a garment: 'She sewed the button on my shirt.' 'On' for location (it's on the shirt). 'Onto' for the action (she attached it onto the shirt). 'In' describes something inside: 'The thread is in the needle.'

lines.text: ❌ "This dress is made of a silk. It's very expensive."

lines.text: ✅ "This dress is made of silk. It's very expensive."
lines.name: ✅ "This dress is made of silk. It's very expensive."

lines.text: Fabric names used as materials don't take 'a': 'made of silk', 'made of cotton', 'made of wool.' The article is used when specifying a particular type: 'a fine silk from China.' But general material: no article. 'The shirt is cotton.' 'The jacket is leather.'

lines.text: ❌ "Can you make this trouser shorter, please?"
lines.name: ❌ "Can you make this trouser shorter, please?"

lines.text: ✅ "Can you make these trousers shorter, please?"
lines.name: ✅ "Can you make these trousers shorter, please?"

lines.text: 'Trousers' is always plural in English: 'these trousers', 'a pair of trousers.' Same for: 'jeans', 'shorts', 'scissors', 'glasses.' 'This pair of trousers is too long.' 'These trousers are too long.' Both are correct.

lines.text: ❌ "He asked me that how much the suit costs."

lines.text: ✅ "He asked me how much the suit costs."

lines.text: Indirect questions don't include 'that' before a question word. 'He asked me how much...' 'She asked where the shop was.' 'They asked when it would be ready.' The pattern is: ask + (person) + question word + statement order. Never 'asked that how' or 'asked that where.'

lines.text: Savile Row in London is the world's most famous street for bespoke tailoring. A 'Savile Row suit' implies the highest quality. 'Bespoke' is a British term meaning custom-made to order — it originally meant 'spoken for' (already reserved by a customer).

lines.text: 'Tailor' traditionally referred to someone who makes men's clothing (suits, jackets). 'Seamstress' = a woman who sews. 'Dressmaker' = someone who makes women's clothes. Today, 'tailor' is used for all genders and all garment types.
lines.name: 'Tailor' traditionally referred to someone who makes men's clothing (suits, jackets). 'Seamstress' = a woman who sews. 'Dressmaker' = someone who makes women's clothes. Today, 'tailor' is used for all genders and all garment types.

lines.text: 'Off the peg' (BrE) / 'off the rack' (AmE) = ready-made in standard sizes. 'Made to measure' = adjusted to your measurements from a standard pattern. 'Bespoke' = created entirely from scratch to your specifications — the most expensive option.

lines.text: 'Sew' /səʊ/ — past: 'sewed', past participle: 'sewn' (not 'sew/sowed'). Don't confuse with 'sow' /saʊ/ (plant seeds). 'Seam' = the line where two pieces of fabric are joined. 'Hem' = the folded edge. 'Dart' = a small fold stitched to shape a garment.
